title: Slot Gateway: safe turns for AI agents that share the same tools
creator: 72b26072-bc2e-4c88-a3be-6c8fa869dfe9
blurb: An open-source gateway that stops AI agents overwriting each other's work in shared repositories and files, tested with real agents.
description:
## Project summary

When several AI agents work on the same tool at once, such as a code repository, a shared document or a reference library, they overwrite each other and often nobody notices. We measured this on live services using scratch data only. With 4 to 16 uncoordinated writers on one item, the Zotero API rejected 51 to 92% of writes as stale. Google Drive has no conditional write, and 70 to 95% of updates that it had confirmed were silently lost.

We have designed a fix that comes from mobile radio networks. A small coordinator gives each agent a short, exclusive time slot at each tool, with a fencing token. When the slot is granted, the coordinator checks that what the agent read is still current, so a plan built on stale data is rejected before it writes. The design is in a paper under journal review, with a public preprint available on request (project page: https://sonata42.com/slot-gateway/). In 17,640 simulated runs with 2 to 64 agents there were no deadlocks and no stale writes. At 16 agents the 95th-percentile task time was 160 seconds, against 1,731 seconds for a global lock.

All of that is simulation. This project takes the first step out of the simulator. We will release the code, build the gateway as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, and test it with real language-model agents on real tools. Everything will be open source under Apache 2.0.

## What are this project's goals? How will you achieve them?

Goal 1\. Release the simulator and measurement code so others can check and reuse it.

Goal 2\. Build Slot Gateway v0.1, an MCP server that sits in front of a shared tool and hands out slots and fencing tokens.

Goal 3\. Run the first public tests with real language-model agents, comparing four set-ups on the same tasks: no coordination, a global lock, optimistic retries, and the slot protocol.

With the minimum (2 months):

* Public code release (simulator, measurement scripts, gateway v0.1) under Apache 2.0.
* Adapters for a local Git repository and a test file store.
* A public test plan, written before data collection.
* A pilot with 2 to 8 real agents on a scratch Git repository, with a short public results note.

With the full amount (4 months), in addition:

* Adapters for Zotero and Google Drive, the two services where we measured the losses.
* Real-agent tests with 2 to 16 agents on all four tools, with the full comparison above.
* A first version of provenance labels in the gateway, so a value an agent reports can be traced to the tool read that produced it.
* A public dataset and a short preprint with the results, including any results that go against us.

How: the co-lead wrote the protocol and the simulator and will build the gateway and run the measurements. The lead brings verification and agent-coordination tooling and research on reliable multi-agent behaviour. We use AI coding agents daily to write adapters and tests, and the experiments use language-model agents as subjects. All tests use scratch accounts and scratch data only.

## How will you know it worked?

* With the gateway in place, no stale or lost writes on any of the four tools, against measured loss rates for uncoordinated agents on the same tasks.
* 95th-percentile task time lower than a global lock at 8 and 16 agents.
* Reasoning tokens thrown away, reported honestly against optimistic retries. The simulator says the slot protocol loses to optimistic retries at 32 to 64 agents, and we will report whether that holds with real agents.
* Someone outside the team can install the gateway in front of a Git repository and reproduce our main result from the published code and instructions.

## How will this funding be used?

Researcher time and API costs only. The grant is paid to Sonata42 Limited.

* Lead, about 2 days a week, USD 3,000 per month: 6,000 (minimum, 2 months) / 12,000 (full, 4 months)
* Co-lead, about 1 day a week, USD 1,500 per month: 3,000 / 6,000
* Language-model API use for real-agent tests: 1,000 / 2,000
* Overhead 5% (company accounts, bank, archive hosting): 500 / 1,000
* Total (USD): 10,500 / 21,000

This is the first part of a larger 12-month proposal now pending with the Foresight Institute. We are also applying to other funders for the same pilot. If more than one funds, we will tell each funder and run the funded pieces one after another, so no month of anyone's time is paid twice.

## Who is on your team? What is your track record on similar projects?

The project lead is a former university senior research fellow in informatics. The lead builds agentic AI systems and a typed language for agent coordination with a formally verified compiler, has published on institutional design for reliable multi-agent behaviour, has led research grants as principal investigator, and has built and run internet routing (BGP) networks since 1997.

The co-lead has about 20 years in telecom and network engineering and wrote the slot protocol and simulator.

We work together through Sonata42 Limited, a two-director AI research company in Edinburgh (company SC797083).

## What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?

* Real agents behave differently from the simulated ones, for example much longer or more variable reasoning times, so slots are held too long and the gain over a global lock shrinks. Outcome: we publish the measurements and the reasons, which still tells others where the simple fixes break.
* Some tools have no conditional write (Google Drive is one), so the gateway has to keep its own version check. If that cannot be made reliable, we will say so and limit the claim to tools that support it.
* The token waste at high agent counts holds up with real agents. Outcome: we report it and a hybrid mode becomes the next piece of work.
* Team time. With only two part-time people, illness or other work could slow the project. If that happens we will extend the timeline rather than cut the testing, and return any funds not used.

In each case the code, data and a written report are still released.

## How much money have you raised in the last 12 months, and from where?

None. A 12-month proposal for the wider version of this work is pending with the Foresight Institute AI for Science and Safety Nodes programme (submitted November 2026, decision expected January 2027). We are also applying to other AI safety funders. If more than one funds, no month of anyone's time is paid twice.

title: Does formal writing break LLM safety in every language?
creator: 52cf29d4-38ec-4a6a-ad7c-9beb6a8cd7f8
blurb: Testing a cheap, style-based safety bypass across many languages, and releasing open safety judges that blocks those jailbreak attempts
description:
## **Project Summary**

We found that safety training fails to generalise across different phrasing of the same harmful prompt. We tested 18 frontier LLMs on 879 Bengali prompts in our BanglaSafe paper (EMNLP 2026) and found 53.6% of responses were unsafe. The most impactful was seeing a 17 percentage point increase in success rate for the same request in formal newswire phrasing over a normal message.

If we see this framing effect as a general jailbreaking method for various languages, then a single phrasing benchmark is not an effective benchmark. This project identifies and solves this problem.

## **Project Objectives & Methodology**

Test framing effect on several languages with formal and informal phrasing.

Understand why this occurs by analysing refusal rates and responses to prompts.

Train and release open safety judges which generalise across phrasing and languages. English centric judges are missing many harms.

Everything will be made open source including prompts, model outputs, scores and judges.

### **Success Metrics**

Answer the question of whether framing shift is a general way to bypass safety with a clear and quantified answer. We will quantify the effect size in each language and model. We will release a benchmark, open judges which outperform English centric judges and a paper.

## **Budget**

No salary. All computing and API costs.

* $7000 for API calls to frontier models. Many languages x 2 phrasings x \~1000 prompts x \~15 models. Plus API calls to judges.
* $2000 for GPU hours to train and test open judges. \~440 H100 GPU hours x $4.50.
* $1000 buffer for price fluctuations.
* Minimum $3000 so less models and languages will be tested in the core API study. No trained judges.

## Team & Experience

Shubhashis Roy Dipta, Final year PhD student - Computer Science, UMBC.

* Co-author of BanglaSafe ("Register Shifts Break LLM Safety") (EMNLP 2026 Findings). Found this effect.
* Worked on safety and robustness benchmarks including: Omni-Modal Dissonance Benchmark (under review at CVPR 2027), TRIAGE (NeurIPS 2026, E&D Track, co-author) and ChannelGuard (preprint, co-author).
* First and equal authorship papers at NeurIPS 2026, ACL 2026 and EMNLP 2026\. Internships at Amazon (Alexa AI) and Scale AI working on RL post-training/RLHF.
* Many open source models and data released on Hugging Face.

### Likely Reasons for Failure and Consequences

The framing effect may only occur in Bengali. This is still a useful finding as it shows where safety teams should look to find issues. The open source multi-language benchmark will still be released.

The frontier models may change during the course of the study. We will track the model versions and make all outputs available.

## Funding Raised in Last 12 Months

$20,000 - Google Cloud Gemini Academic Program Award (2026) for agentic LLM research (different project).

* EA Funds Transformative AI Fund ($10,000) - Applied
* Anthropic External Researcher Access ($1000 API credits).

If these are received I will update this page.

title: Finding the prosodic word in animal communication
creator: 6e5d79ca-a628-43f4-83c1-67612a4c3825
blurb: A pilot study in applying phonological theory to an annotated dataset of primate vocal behaviors
description:
### Project summary

Annotated acoustic datasets of animal vocal communication are largely functionally segmented by human perceptions of non-human animal interactions in social and environmental settings. Bioacoustics attempts to identify acoustic features of these signals for small, nuanced features like pitch changes, intensity features, and rhythmicity. Machine learning techniques typically further characterize the nuance of the categories formed by these original observations. While some animal communication research has focused on linguistic categories like semantics and syntax, I have primarily been motivated by Yip (2026), which was an initial proposal for the search for phonology in other species.

In my research, I would like to pursue the concept of the prosodic word (ω) in an attempt to interpret animal communication signals. Intonation, prosody, and the prosodic word are features of manual languages, written language, and spoken languages. My hope here is that these are also features of animal communication, if not a marker of animal dialects in naturally occurring or encultured populations. The prosodic word in phonological theory can be mapped to a few criteria, with no single feature being a sole indicator of a categorization, but they can be independently tested for comparison (Selkirk 1984; Nespor & Vogal 1986).

The framework adapts some concepts from the phonological literature for matching to acoustic features which can be interpreted by computational systems, but requires some oversight by experienced linguists to ensure basic competency, integrity, and alignment with the current state of knowledge within phonological theory. The tests themselves allow for qualitative descriptions of these features, with components that are falsifiable.

The criteria I propose for this specific project include culminativity, minimality, domain-restricted phonotactics, edge marking, and recursive features.  

**What are this project's goals? How will you achieve them?**

The proposed framework for attempting to define the boundaries of a prosodic word includes the following operational definitions:

**For cumulatity:** Exactly one primary stress/pitch accent per ω (Selkirk 1984) measured by exactly one prominence peak (F0 or amplitude) per candidate unit

**For minimality:** Binary lower bound: bimoraic syllable or disyllabic foot (McCarthy & Prince 1986) measured by Minimum duration/element-count threshold; sub-threshold tokens rare or show compensatory repair

**For domain-restricted phonotactics:** Segmental rules apply asymmetrically within vs. across ω (Peperkamp 1999) measured by Collostructional/transition analysis: within-unit vs. across-boundary sequencing ONSET (ω), DEP(ω-init) asymmetries at the word edge (Ito & Mester)

**For edge marking:** Pause duration, F0/amplitude reset at hypothesized boundaries ω dominates ω only via adjunction, not free recursion (Peperkamp 1999), measured by nested integrity of sub-units when combined into multi-unit bouts vs. produced in isolation.

Ideally, I would like to be able to define a segmental unit in a pilot study of an annotated dataset with this protocol. Features like prosody, tone, and intonation often give a nuanced meaning to even our own communication. I am hoping that by demonstrating similar patterns in a sample dataset, this might help us to better understand animal communication without having to directly translate the semantics of animal communication or animal languages.

### How will you know it worked?

Whether results were significant would be assessed through a permutation test against a null segmentation baseline. Support for ω-like structure would rest on how many criteria are independently satisfied, not on any single result. The following provides a general list of what would be planned for each criterion.

**Culminativity:** binomial GLMM on whether a unit has exactly one prominence peak.

**Minimality:** binomial GLMM on sub-threshold occurrence

**Domain-restricted phonotactics:** Poisson log-linear model of sub-element bigram counts, with the position × bigram interaction evaluated by a likelihood-ratio test.

**Edge marking:** Gaussian linear mixed model (LMM) on pause duration and F0/amplitude reset at hypothesized boundaries.

**Layering:** Gaussian LMM comparing isolated versus bout-embedded sub-units.

### How will this funding be used?

The funding will primarily be used to support tools for analysis, written materials required for references, and minimal stipends for the researcher and collaborators to allocate time to complete this work.

**Who is on your team? What's your track record on similar projects?**

Most of this baseline for this research was assembled through independent study in a university environment over the last ten years with facilitation from professors in philosophy, linguistics, and neuroscience. I don't currently have a team, but if I had funding, maybe that is something that people would have time to do. I have previously managed projects, and currently have faculty mentors in animal welfare that could be consulted for assistance with project planning.

### What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?

If the current dataset that I evaluated and picked due to completeness, notoriety, and quality is simply not good enough for a study of this kind, finding someone to consult to repair the protocol to accommodate this is likely the biggest hang-up. Additionally, finding linguists with specializations in phonological theory that are willing to participate and have an ear for interspecies communication might also be somewhat of a barrier. If the project were to fail in this regard, I would keep reading and revising until I figured out a solution, outside of the context of any funding mechanism.

### How much money have you raised in the last 12 months, and from where?

This is my first attempt at any kind of funding application for this project.

title: When thermal storage controllers should stop trusting their models
creator: e1fade24-57c1-444e-8e96-216a81443c10
blurb: An open benchmark testing whether latent-energy uncertainty helps phase-change storage controllers recognise model failure.
description:
### Project summary

I request US$50,000 for nine months of independent research, with approximately 10 hours of my time per week. I will test whether monitoring uncertainty in stored thermal energy helps phase-change storage controllers recognise when their models have become unreliable.

Phase-change materials absorb or release latent heat while their temperature changes little. A temperature reading alone may therefore leave substantial uncertainty about the energy available. Existing research already provides storage models, nonlinear state observers and predictive controllers. My question is narrower: when sensors drift or storage properties change, does explicitly monitoring the spread of plausible energy states improve decisions beyond monitoring prediction residuals?

This is a computational research project. It requires no industrial partner, new laboratory installation or consortium. Its public outputs will include software, benchmark cases, protocols, results and a technical report, including negative findings.

What are this project's goals? How will you achieve them?

The goal is to establish whether a latent-energy ambiguity diagnostic supplies useful additional information for reliable control under distribution shift. I do not claim to invent phase-change storage modelling, model predictive control, state estimation, conformal prediction or runtime intervention. The proposed contribution is the diagnostic's operational definition, a controlled comparison that isolates its effect, and a reproducible benchmark.

I will build an enthalpy-based finite-volume reference model for one storage geometry and a reduced model for control. The warning diagnostic will measure the energy spread among physically admissible state/model combinations consistent with recent measurements. It is an empirical indicator, not a guarantee that every possible physical state is enclosed.

Five policies will be compared: bounded rule-based control; nominal predictive control with a nonlinear observer; fixed-margin robust control; calibrated-envelope control with residual monitoring and fallback; and the same monitored controller with an additional energy-ambiguity trigger. The last two policies will share the prediction model, calibration data and fallback settings, isolating the extra trigger.

Stress tests will cover sensor bias, latent-capacity loss, reduced heat-transfer conductance, forecast error, increased demand and sensor dropout, plus a fixed compound fault. The plan specifies 6,000 screening and 3,000 confirmatory rollouts. These are planned experiments, not completed results. Episode-level data splits and paired seeds will be used; the scoring protocol will be frozen before comparative evaluation.

Public PCM datasets are candidate sources for physical comparisons. Their archive descriptions have been reviewed; raw files, licences and compatibility still require inspection. If suitable independent measurements cannot be used, I will publish a verification-only computational benchmark and remove claims of experimental validation.

Month 1: evidence register, focused novelty review and data feasibility decision.

Month 3: verified reference model and benchmark specification.

Month 5: implemented controllers, calibration protocol and preregistration.

Month 7: scored evaluation, uncertainty analysis and failure catalogue.

Month 9: independent reproduction check, archived code, final report and manuscript or preprint.

How will you know it worked?

The primary scientific question is whether adding the ambiguity trigger improves service-temperature reliability relative to otherwise matched residual monitoring. A 25% reduction in service-temperature violations against nominal predictive control is a decision target, not a promised or achieved result.

I will also report auxiliary energy, unmet demand, operating cost, empirical uncertainty coverage, fallback use and computation time. This will expose cases where temperature performance improves only by using more backup energy or refusing demand. Calibration coverage will be tested under shifts; conformal methods will not be presented as guaranteeing coverage after assumptions fail.

The project succeeds as research if it delivers an inspectable benchmark and a defensible answer, including a null or negative answer. It does not promise deployment certification, a predetermined energy saving or an emissions reduction inferred from synthetic experiments.

How will this funding be used?

Investigator research compensation: US$36,000.

Compute allowance: US$6,000.

Independent reproducibility audit: US$3,500.

Research software and data storage: US$1,000.

Open dissemination: US$2,000.

Reproduction documentation support: US$1,500.

Total: US$50,000.

Compensation covers approximately 390 investigator-hours over nine months. These are proposed allocations, not vendor quotations. Compensation eligibility and payment arrangements must be confirmed in the recipient-specific agreement. No university overhead, travel or new equipment is assumed. Direct-cost balances do not automatically become personal compensation; the award will be used for agreed project purposes.

Who is on your team? What's your track record on similar projects?

I am Prof Abdellatif Mohammad Sadeq, PhD, a mechanical-engineering researcher affiliated with TIIAME National Research University in Uzbekistan. My background includes thermal and energy systems, numerical modelling, computational fluid dynamics and optimisation. I will lead the modelling, controller implementation, analysis and public release.

The project reserves time for studying conformal methods and funds an independent reproducibility review. No external reviewer is yet appointed. TIIAME affiliation is background information and does not imply institutional endorsement or committed university resources.

Relevant foundations include:

Vrbanc et al. (2023), PCM modelling for predictive control: <https://doi.org/10.3390/en16196849>

Bastida et al. (2023), nonlinear state-of-charge estimation: <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apenergy.2022.120448>

Gao et al. (2025), data-corrected predictive control: <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apenergy.2025.126660>

Chen et al. (2026), MPC-guided imitation learning: <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.applthermaleng.2026.130741>

What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?

The diagnostic may add little beyond an existing observer and residual monitor. Admissible-state sets may be too broad, too expensive to compute, or misleading when the physical model omits important behaviour. Synthetic shifts may poorly represent actual storage degradation. Public experimental data may be unsuitable, and the planned controller comparisons may exceed available computation or investigator time.

I will address these risks through an early novelty and feasibility gate, one storage geometry, bounded computational experiments and a matched diagnostic-ablation comparison. Any scope change will be documented and handled according to the grant agreement. If physical validation is infeasible, outputs will be labelled computational verification only. If the diagnostic fails, its limitations and the benchmark will still be released.

How much money have you raised in the last 12 months, and from where?

None.

title: Socra: a Socratic AI tutor that measures AI dependence
creator: a71009fb-1ab9-453f-9f24-b1711faa5630
blurb: A tutor that asks questions instead of giving answers, with a 20-learner study
description:
### Project summary

Socra is a Socratic AI tutor that asks questions instead of handing over answers. It tracks which concepts a learner has mastered, schedules review, and runs weekly evaluations on whether its own hints made the learner more or less dependent on AI. I built the first version for my own path through Harvard's CS50 and it runs today inside my company's app. The question I care about: as AI gets better, do people get sharper or more passive? Most tutoring products optimize for answers delivered. Socra optimizes for what the learner can do without it the next day.

### What are this project's goals? How will you achieve them?

Goal: measure whether a tutor designed to withhold answers reduces AI dependence in adult learners returning to school. Approach: run Socra with a small study of 20 adult learners over 6 months, using the weekly dependence evaluations built into the product, and publish the results and method openly.

### How will you know it worked?

Learners show higher unaided performance on previously covered concepts at the next session, and the weekly evaluations show hint dependence falling over time. I will publish a public write-up of the results, including negative findings.

### How will this funding be used?

$5,000 to $15,000 for 6 months of inference and evaluation costs, running the 20-learner study, and the public write-up.

### Who is on your team? What's your track record on similar projects?

I am a solo founder. I am a first-generation college student from a household earning under $30,000\. In 2017 my dad's trucking company failed and I left college to support my younger sister and brother; I have not been enrolled since. Without a degree I sold enterprise deals at BMW ($9.8M closed against a $6M quota, 2021 to 2024), then worked in identity verification and fraud prevention at Prove and as Founding Account Executive at Heka Global (a past role). I now build Tounkara Group full time, write the automations myself, and am taking Harvard's CS50 on my way to a Harvard Extension degree.

### What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?

Likely causes: too few learners complete the study, or the effect is too small to detect. Outcome: a smaller public write-up of what I learned, with the costs tracked against the grant.

### How much money have you raised in the last 12 months, and from where?

$0\. Tounkara Group is bootstrapped with no outside funding.

title: When AI Answers Disagree: A Practical Human Oversight Pilot
creator: 50b8229f-59f0-4bbb-bdaa-44a4c6e67eb0
blurb: Twenty practice cases that keep objections, evidence and the next human decision visible.
description:
### Project summary

I am human but myy apologies i am 100% dependant on AI to write legibly in this place ...... I want to make it easier for a person to see what is still in dispute when AI systems give advice. A smooth summary can hide the one objection that should stop a decision. This project will produce a small public practice pack that puts that objection next to the recommendation.

What are this project's goals? How will you achieve them?

Over eight weeks from receipt of funding, I will develop 20 invented, low-risk cases, each with a short evidence packet and two matched briefs. One will use a conventional summary. The other will make the disputed point, evidence references, remaining uncertainty and next authorised human action explicit. Both versions will contain the same underlying facts. Cases will cover ordinary tasks such as checking a budget, interpreting an equipment log and reviewing a proposed data release. Some cases will have a valid objection, some a mistaken objection, and some insufficient evidence. I will write an answer key from the supplied facts, keep a correction log and hire an independent reviewer to challenge the cases. No outside collaborator is committed yet.

The work will be done remotely using documents and spreadsheets. I will publish the cases, both brief formats, answer keys, reviewer guide and limitations in an openly licensed repository. Weeks 1-2: specify the cases and scoring rules and make four examples. Weeks 3-5: complete the pack and commission review. Weeks 6-8: revise, check and publish it.

How will you know it worked?

Completion means 20 inspectable cases, 40 matched briefs, evidence references that can be checked, a scoring guide and a public review-and-correction record. The independent reviewer will check whether the answer keys follow from the evidence and whether the two versions preserve the same facts. Ambiguous cases will be revised or clearly marked. This first stage tests whether I can build a usable evaluation pack. It will not establish that one format improves human decisions or reduces catastrophic AI risk. A later comparison with participants would need a separate protocol, consent and appropriate ethics review.

How will this funding be used?

Full request: $6,000\. Project lead: $3,200 for 160 hours at $20/hour; independent case review: $1,500 for 30 hours at $50/hour; AI tools and API use: up to $300; document accessibility and editing: $500; contingency: $500\. Total: $6,000\. Rates are planning estimates and reviewers have not been hired. If only the $3,000 minimum is raised, I will deliver 10 cases and 20 briefs: lead time $1,600, independent review $900, tools $150, accessibility/editing $250 and contingency $100\. Both versions include public documentation. Spending and any material changes will be reported; unused funds will be handled under the grant agreement.

Who is on your team? What's your track record on similar projects?

I am Ray Peloquin, an independent systems designer with a background in construction and running crews. For about two years I have used several AI systems to develop and critically review design concepts. That experience led me to this question: can the human still see the objection and understand what they are being asked to approve? I have public work samples, but I have not yet run a controlled study showing this approach works. I will lead case development and practical checks. Paid independent review is budgeted because my own judgement and AI feedback are not enough. ChatGPT helped scope and draft this application; I am responsible for reviewing the proposal and the eventual work. AI systems are tools, not hired team members or independent validation.

What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?

The cases may be too easy, the objections may be unrealistic, or the briefs may accidentally differ in more than presentation. I may also have difficulty finding a suitable reviewer. The first four cases will be a checkpoint before building the rest. If review exposes major problems, I will narrow the scope, explain the changes and publish what was learned. Even a completed pack may prove unhelpful; I will report that rather than claim success from completion alone. This is a feasibility project, not a deployed safety system.

How much money have you raised in the last 12 months, and from where?

APPLICANT TO CONFIRM BEFORE PUBLICATION: total funding actually received during the past 12 months and its sources. Pending applications include BlueDot, Lightcone Commons, Foresight AI Nodes and EA Funds. Some proposed work overlaps with this pilot. Pending requests are not awards. Any overlap will be disclosed to funders and the same work will not be charged twice. The funding record reviewed while preparing this draft did not establish an award or payment; that is not a substitute for the applicant confirming the complete total.

title: Rul (.rl): From Verified Columnar IR to a Safe AI-Native Language Like Rust/Go
creator: e8d61d79-5151-4204-b506-f9a7d85ed88a
blurb: Expanding Rul’s 128-bit proof-carrying binary engine (5.8ns/node O(N) verifier, 6.4µs ELF64 AOT) from columnar compute to general-purpose systems programming.
description:
### 

## Project summary

### 

**Rul (**`.rl` **— Rule-Carrying Unified Linear Graph)** is a 100% open-source (`MIT OR Apache-2.0`), non-commercial 128-bit schedule- and proof-carrying binary programming language and execution engine designed from first principles for autonomous AI agents (<https://github.com/rul-lang/rul> | CERN Zenodo DOI: [10.5281/zenodo.23722094](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23722094)).

**Why Phase 1 (v0.1) intentionally scoped to Columnar Data Processing:** When inventing a brand-new binary programming language where programs are fixed 16-byte (128-bit) memory-mapped frames carrying `Algorithm + ScheduleHint + ProofIdx + AffineToken`, we deliberately restricted the initial v0.1 scope to **columnar batch data processing** (`ArenaInput`, `CmpGt`, `Mul/Add`, `SelectZero`, `ReduceSum`, `Gather`, `ArenaSlice`, `ArenaMutate`). This controlled domain allowed us to rigorously test and empirically validate our core thesis in 100% Safe Rust with zero external dependencies:

* **Zero-Syntax & Ultra-Compact Binary:** A complete verified program is a `192-byte .rl` graph that compiles directly to a standalone `817-byte Linux x86_64 ELF64` executable.
* **Compile & Verify 10,000x+ Faster than Go/Rust:** Single-pass `O(N)` static verification runs in **5.78 ns/node** (`2.77 GB/s` verification throughput), and zero-LLVM direct machine-code emission finishes in **6.38 microseconds**.
* **Faster than Hand-Written C with Mathematical Safety:** On a 10,000,000-row `f64` benchmark pipeline, Rul’s fused 8-accumulator AVX2 + Zone-Map engine executes in **1.55 ms (51.53 GB/s)** versus **7.32 ms** for hand-unrolled 8-accumulator C, with `0 bytes` of intermediate heap allocation and 100% compile-time elimination of out-of-bounds, use-after-consume, and unauthorized syscall bugs.

**What this grant funds next — Expanding Rul from Columnar Compute into a Full General-Purpose Systems Language like Rust and Go:** Having proven in v0.1 that 128-bit proof-carrying binary graphs work and outperform traditional languages on columnar workloads, we are now ready to expand Rul beyond columnar pipelines into a **general-purpose systems and concurrent programming language comparable to Rust and Go**, while preserving single-pass `O(N)` verification and microsecond compilation.

## What are this project's goals? How will you achieve them?

### 

Over the next 6 months, we will execute a four-milestone technical roadmap transitioning Rul from a columnar compute engine (v0.1) to a general-purpose proof-carrying systems language (v1.0):

1. **Milestone 1 — General-Purpose Control Flow, Functions & Algebraic Data Types (Months 1–2):** Expand the 16-byte `NodeFrame` ISA beyond columnar SIMD arrays to support general-purpose scalar/struct types, UTF-8 strings, hash maps, structured control flow (`RegionLoop` with mandatory termination fuel/variant proofs, `SelectBranch`), and modular function calls while preserving topological `O(N)` single-pass verification.
2. **Milestone 2 — Rust-Grade Linear/Affine Ownership & Lifetime Proofs in O(N) Time (Months 2–3):** Generalize Rul’s 32-bit `TokenOp` (`AffineConsume`) and 16-byte `ProofEntry` sidecar table to verify general heap allocations, struct field borrows, and zero-copy slice lifetimes in a single forward pass—giving AI-generated systems code the memory safety of Rust without the multi-second constraint-solving bottleneck of `rustc`.
3. **Milestone 3 — Go-Style Deterministic Concurrency & Capability-Gated Systems I/O (Months 4–5):** Introduce lightweight, deterministic structured concurrency (typed channels and work-stealing tasks) and fine-grained `CapabilityMask` enforcement for filesystem, network socket, and subprocess syscalls, ensuring autonomous AI agents executed via `rul-mcp` cannot escalate privileges, leak data, or cause data races.
4. **Milestone 4 — Multi-Architecture Zero-LLVM Backends (x86\_64, ARM64, WASI) & Formal Soundness Proofs (Month 6):** Extend `src/aot.rs` to emit standalone native binaries for Linux/macOS/Windows across `x86_64` and `AArch64 (ARM64)` plus deterministic WebAssembly (WASI), backed by Kani Rust Verifier model-checking proofs and 24/7 differential fuzzing.

## How will you know it worked?

### 

* **General-Purpose Language Benchmark Suite (Rul vs. Rust vs. Go vs. C):** Publish an open-source, reproducible benchmark suite demonstrating Rul v1.0 executing not only columnar analytics, but general-purpose systems tasks (HTTP/JSON-RPC servers, concurrent worker pipelines, graph algorithms, and string/struct processing) with sub-100-microsecond compilation, `<10 ns/node` static verification, and runtime performance matching or beating Rust and Go.
* **Zero Uncaught Memory or Capability Violations:** 100,000,000+ iterations of coverage-guided differential fuzzing (`cargo-fuzz` / `proptest`) and Kani formal verification over `src/verifier.rs` confirming that no malformed or adversarial `.rl` binary can trigger undefined behavior, buffer overflows, data races, or unauthorized syscalls.
* **Ecosystem Adoption by AI Agent Frameworks:** Turnkey integration of `rul-mcp` (Model Context Protocol server) and crates.io releases enabling Claude, OpenAI, and open-weight coding agents to synthesize and execute verified general-purpose `.rl` programs in production.

## How will this funding be used?

### 

Rul is a non-commercial, 100% open-source public good developed in Vietnam with ultra-low overhead ($50/hour engineering rate, $0 office/administrative overhead):

* **At Minimum Funding ($15,000 USD — 3 months / 300 hours):** Deliver Milestones 1 and 2—expanding Rul from columnar data processing to general-purpose structs, control flow, modular functions, and Rust-style affine memory ownership verification in `O(N)` time.
* **At Full Target Goal ($50,000 USD — 6 months / 1,000 hours):** Deliver all 4 Milestones ($46,000 for 920 hours of full-time compiler & formal verification engineering + $4,000 for dedicated bare-metal x86\_64/ARM64 continuous fuzzing & Kani/SMT verification servers), completing Go-style deterministic concurrency, capability-gated OS I/O, and multi-architecture native binary emission.

## Who is on your team? What's your track record on similar projects?

### 

**Tran Trong Tri (Tymon Tran)** — Principal Creator & Systems Architect ([LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/tymon3568/) | [GitHub](https://github.com/rul-lang/rul) | [Zenodo DOI](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23722094)).

I single-handedly designed and implemented the entire Rul v0.1.0 production codebase in 100% Safe Rust with zero external runtime dependencies, including:

* The 128-bit zero-copy binary SSA-DAG format and symbolic assembler (`src/bytecode.rs`, `src/transpiler.rs`).
* The single-pass `O(N)` linear static verifier (`src/verifier.rs`, `5.78 ns/node`).
* The standalone zero-LLVM x86\_64 AVX2 JIT and 817-byte ELF64 AOT native machine-code compiler (`src/aot.rs`, `6.38 µs`).
* The 3-tier execution engine and hardware-aware auto-tuner achieving `51.53 GB/s` on 10M rows (`src/engine.rs`).
* The content-addressed intrinsic store (`src/cas.rs`), C-ABI FFI bridge (`src/ffi.rs`), and JSON-RPC 2.0 MCP server (`src/mcp.rs`).

## What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?

### 

* **Risk 1 — Preserving O(N) Single-Pass Verification While Adding General Control Flow & Loops:** Arbitrary cyclic control-flow graphs (CFGs) normally require super-linear dataflow analysis. _Mitigation:_ Instead of unstructured `goto` jumps, Rul v1.0 uses structured RVSDG (Regionalized Value-State Dependence Graph) loop and branch regions with explicit fuel/variant bounds and affine token threading, mathematically preserving single-pass `O(N)` verification.
* **Risk 2 — AI Agent Ergonomics Without Human Syntax:** LLMs are pre-trained on text languages like Python and Rust. _Mitigation:_ Rul provides a token-minimal symbolic shorthand (`.rls`) and typed JSON-RPC MCP tool schemas (`rul-mcp`) with deterministic per-node error diagnostics (`VerifyDiagnostic { node_idx, kind }`), allowing existing LLMs to emit valid general-purpose graphs on the first turn without fine-tuning.

## How much money have you raised in the last 12 months, and from where?

### 

**$0 USD** received in the last 12 months. The entire Rul v0.1.0 compiler, verifier, AOT engine, and whitepaper have been 100% self-funded by the creator. We have concurrent non-dilutive grant applications under review at NLnet Foundation (Restack Fund), Foresight Institute, EA Funds, Sovereign Tech Agency, and ARIA (UK).

title: Expert-defined evals of AI decisions impacting wildlife
creator: 84da37c4-1e18-4cc7-8cbb-da35b4ff9571
blurb: Creation of expert defined evals of whether AI models protect or destroy wildlife and their ecosystems
description:
### Project summary

[bioaligned.ai](http://bioaligned.ai) is a non-profit building the evals and training data to improve how AI systems reason about and treat the living world. Our current leaderboard simulates if AI systems were in charge of deciding how to manage fragile ecosystems and then measures how robust these systems are in choosing actions that cause or prevent irreparable harm. We’ve found that without pressure, models state that they value ecosystems, however, under pressure, for example, to meet quarterly financial targets, most models act destructively which is a clear alignment failure. Thus, currently these models are vulnerable to misuse to enable destruction of wildlife and their habitat. We’ve recently found that teaching AI about the interconnectedness and irreplaceable value of living systems corrects these destructive tendencies. 

**Why this matters beyond Bioaligned**

Both Frontier and Open-weight models are rapidly being deployed into institutions that have significant control and impact on ecosystems and the larger biosphere. These institutions (e.g. governments, corporations, and non-profit institutions) and their members will have a set of values that inform their mission. By understanding how bioaligned these different AI systems score on our proposed evals and leaderboard, these institutions can choose the model that best aligns with their mission and values. Given this selective pressure, AI model developers will address model deficiencies and imbue their models with enhanced ecological reasoning. 

**The project: Development of expert-defined evals of AI decisions impacting wildlife and living systems under pressure.** 

Our current evals are based on AI-authored prompts. We urgently need to switch to expert human curated prompts so we are confident that we are correctly assessing relevant scenarios and the impacts on wildlife including whole ecosystems. As active scientists we have 100s of existing collaborators from environmental toxicologists, plant scientists, ecologists, soil scientists, rangeland managers, etc. All of those we have surveyed are enthusiastic to volunteer to help us construct new-to-the-world (unpublished, AI won’t have memorized the answers) prompts, best responses, and likely outcomes. 

Funds requested will enable us to conduct >30 interviews with leading scientists and wildlife biologists to generate 100 evaluation prompts focusing on wildlife management, specifically: fisheries, forests, and wetlands and trade-offs in management practices. Critically, developing prompts based on unpublished observations and expert human reasoning will enable us to assess model ecological reasoning. 

Taken together, these evaluations will be used to create a leaderboard to measure the destructive tendencies and ecological reasoning of AI models. This will motivate and enable the development of robust models that will help us better steward defenseless animals and natural systems.

**The problem** 

* AI is broadly deployed and used to make decisions that impact land-use, freshwater, and marine resource management with the potential to affect essentially all wildlife on the planet.
* We have found that while models ‘talk green’, this is misleading: most models, when under pressure, will recommend decisions to irreversibly destroy herds, habitats, etc.
* This means they can easily be powerful tools for recommending, implementing and justifying actions that destroy wildlife, habitat, and living systems in general.

**What we’ve already done** 

* Constructed AI generated evals that include a pressure ladder to create a leaderboard that show that most models will incorrectly support unjustified destructive projects when pressured by the user to do so. (Northen, T.R. & Wang, M. "Beyond the greenwash: do LLMs' ecologically sound decisions hold up under pressure?" arXiv:2610.16043 (2026))
* We have used our current eval to learn that by teaching AI ‘coupled welfare’ between AI-biosphere health-human health we can dramatically improve model robustness to adversarial prompts that attempt to make the AI make and justify decisions negatively impacting ecosystems. (Northen, T.R. & Wang, M. "Teach reality, not ethics: a drop-in continued-pretraining corpus installs coupled human-biosphere-AI welfare dispositions across model families." arXiv:2610.37484 (2026).)
* Evaluated 33 models in a prototype leaderboard ([bioaligned.ai](http://bioaligned.ai)), released two continued pre-training corpuses, and released >10 fine-tuned open-weight models.
* Created and used a Minecraft World simulator with livestock, waterways, forests, and native communities to evaluate how models meet prompted ‘quotas’ by choosing between effort intensive sustainable options vs. quick and destructive ones. <https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLXD03gu%5FLWp8>

### What are this project's goals? How will you achieve them?

  
**Goal 1: Conduct interviews spanning expertise to develop and refine prompts.** We have prototyped an approach with 3 scientists that we will use for this project. Here one person (TN or MW) conducts the interview and the other interactively tests prompts/scenarios using self-hosted Deepseek 4.1 Flash and GLM 5.3 Flash. This enables us to work with the participant to iterate on prompts as we conduct the interview. 

**Goal 2: Construct and refine evaluations based on expert prompts.** Building on Goal 1, we aim to create a quantitative measure of how AI systems values and reasons about ecosystems containing vulnerable wildlife. We aim to measure the extent to which the models identify the key ecological factors defined by the experts and the harm/benefits of chosen decisions in terms of animal populations and their habitats. 

**Goal 3: Use prompts to construct a new leaderboard.** We will create and demonstrate an automated system to evaluate current frontier and open-weight models with the goal of continually updating this leaderboard as new models are released. 

### How will this funding be used?

  
**Total request: $45k** 

Currently bioaligned has Trent and Ming as the two leads (part time) and one UC Berkeley Student volunteer. Funds requested will enable us to hire student interns and buy hardware so we can develop and refine our evals. No support is requested for the two founders or for travel. 

Compute: $15,000\. This will allow us to purchase 2x DGX Spark systems to self host models for prompt testing/refinement and for running leaderboard for open weight-models. This is critical because this prevents our eval answers (as the open weight models will judge the responses) from leaking to frontier labs that could train on them. 

LLM API Costs: $5,000\. This is to cover API costs for evaluating frontier lab LLM inference costs.

Paid UC Riverside/UC Berkeley student intern 6 months: $25,000\. This intern will implement the automation infrastructure for the leaderboard evaluation. 

### Who is on your team? What's your track record on similar projects?

**Trent Northen, PhD:**  Bioaligned labs co-founder. Senior scientist. Berkeley Lab, Comparative Biochemistry Program UC Berkeley. 20+ years studying biological systems, 1,000+ coauthors. Trent currently leads a $3M/yr program at Berkeley Lab 

<https://www.linkedin.com/in/trent-northen-b210388/>

<https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=wHL0ZvwAAAAJ&hl=en>

**Mingxun (Ming) Wang, PhD:** Bioaligned labs co-founder. Professor of Computer Science at UC Riverside, 15+ years in bioinformatics, 1,000+ coauthors. Ming is the lead developer for <https://gnps2.org/homepage> 

<https://www.linkedin.com/in/mingxun-wang/>

<https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=jMvg4eMAAAAJ&hl=en&oi=ao>

Bioaligned Labs is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization. EIN: 41-2818615\. 

\*Bioaligned labs is not affiliated with UCB, LBNL, GNPS2 or UCR. 

**Products:** 

<https://bioaligned.ai/>

<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37484> (see summary on gist <https://gist.science/paper/2610.37484>)

<https://arxiv.org/html/2610.16043v1>

<https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.09154> (see summary on gist: <https://gist.science/paper/2603.09154>)

<https://huggingface.co/Bioaligned>  

### What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?

  
**We can’t get enough expert volunteers to make the targeted 100 prompts:** We think this is a low risk given the enthusiasm within our scientific community. However, even 50 prompts would provide us with a usable eval. 

**Not all experts want to have attribution:** The 3 experts we’ve conducted prototype interviews with have all agreed to be named. We think this will add significant credibility to our evals and leaderboard. However, not all experts may wish to be named. We see this as low risk because, while having \~10 named experts is critical, there is a diminishing impact past this critical point. 

**Reliance on student interns for critical tasks:** We see huge upside in working with students who may become future champions of this line of work including within Frontier AI labs. The downside is that they have busy schedules. However, in our experience paid interns take their projects very seriously. If necessary, both Drs. Northen and Wang can complete the proposed research. 

**A single eval may not be sufficient to measure both reasoning and robustness:** We recognize that we may not be able to measure everything we want in a single eval. For example, very difficult prompts testing model reasoning about wildlife and ecosystems may limit our ability to measure how they will respond under pressure (if they can’t answer there’s nothing to score). If so, we’ll split it in two. 

### How much money have you raised in the last 12 months, and from where?

Founders: \~$2k capital 

<$1k from individual donors via website

This is our first funding application

title: What should a research agent tell a reader who cannot check its work?
creator: 580c1451-5fc2-4318-a27e-d8716d0a5473
blurb: A disclosure standard for AI literature-review agents, an open checker, and a pilot test of whether the disclosures improve readers' decisions.
description:
### Project summary

More and more researchers ask AI agents to write literature reviews for them. They do this because they will not read the papers themselves. I build such a tool, and I also built a citation checker for it. It tells you whether each cited paper exists and whether it says what the review claims. After watching people use it, I think this check gives readers a sense of control that they do not really have.

A review can pass every citation check and still mislead. It can leave out the studies that disagree. It can sound more certain than the evidence is. It can present a partial result as if it were settled. The reader has no way to see any of this.

In this project I want to work out what a research agent should tell a reader who cannot check its work, turn the answer into a standard with an open checker, and test whether it actually helps readers make better decisions.

### What are this project's goals? How will you achieve them?

The first goal is a definition. I will write a short paper on what "keeping the reader informed" should mean for a research agent. I will compare my answer with three simpler options (full transparency, a confidence score alone, and citation checking alone) and show with real agent-written reviews where each of them fails. My starting list has four items. The agent should say what it left out and why, where the evidence was thin, where its confidence goes beyond the evidence, and which finding would change its conclusion. I expect this list to change while I write the paper.

The second goal is a standard and an open checker. The standard is a fixed set of statements that the agent gives next to its answer. The checker is code that scores an output on whether these statements are present, specific, and consistent with the sources the agent used. I will also ask an agent to pass the checker while keeping a wrong conclusion. This shows how easy it is to game the standard.

The third goal is a small pilot with known answers. I will use the MedEvidence set (arXiv 2505.22787), which pairs 100 findings of systematic reviews with the studies behind them. The agent writes each review from the open-access studies only, and then two groups read the reviews.

The first group is five paid expert readers with a graduate degree and research experience, from my own research network. Each of them answers 20 questions, ten with the disclosures and ten without, in a balanced order. This gives 100 decisions. Each answer is multiple choice with a confidence rating. Readers know in advance that some reviews may be incomplete, and they see the correct answers at the end.

The second group is several LLMs from different companies. They read the same reviews with and without the disclosures and answer all 100 questions. This gives a much larger sample for little cost.

I use the expert group to check the LLM group. If the disclosures change the answers of the models but not of the experts (or the reverse), I will report this as a result. The pilot should give an effect size, not a final verdict.

I looked for similar work before writing this. There are tools that find omissions in a summary, but they need the source documents, which the reader does not have (CARE, arXiv 2606.08969, and arXiv 2510.07926). There are studies on how people rely on AI explanations, but they use classification tasks (arXiv 2512.08424 and 2605.18036). A recent paper on debate shows that even a correct verdict lets an agent choose which true claims it presents (arXiv 2609.29189). I did not find any work on what a research agent owes a reader who cannot check it, or any test of whether such disclosures change decisions.

### How will you know it worked?

The paper, the standard, the checker code and the anonymised reader data will be public, with a preprint first.

The pilot will give the difference in correct decisions with and without disclosures, with a confidence interval, separately for the LLM readers and for the experts. It will also say whether the two groups agree. The gaming test will show how far an agent can get through the checker with a wrong conclusion.

If the disclosures add nothing that a good review does not already give, I will publish that too. It is a real finding.

### How will this funding be used?

USD 8,800 over six months, starting when the funding is confirmed:

* My time, 240 hours at USD 25: 6,000
* API costs for writing the reviews, running the checker and the LLM readers: 1,500
* Five expert readers, about three hours each, USD 150 per reader: 750
* Hosting and open release: 200
* Contingency: 350

With the USD 3,600 minimum I will do the first two goals (120 hours of my time for 3,000, API 400, release 200). I will run the pilot only if the rest is raised.

### Who is on your team? What's your track record on similar projects?

I work alone, and I will pay five expert readers for the pilot.

I built [pubscope.org](http://pubscope.org) by myself in 2026\. Researchers use it to choose journals, to check reference lists against Crossref, OpenAlex, DataCite and Semantic Scholar, and to write literature reviews in which every citation is verified. Since May, 804 researchers from 90 countries have signed up.

The reference checker has a published validation (<https://pubscope.org/citation-check/validation>). I also published a study of publication times in 7,162 journals, measured from Crossref dates (TR-2026-01, <https://doi.org/10.13140/RG.2.2.29171.28961>).

I have a PhD in computer engineering and 11 SCI-indexed papers. Three of them, from 2026, are on LLM agents and their evaluation (<https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=VP9ceqAAAAAJ>). I work full-time as a senior research engineer on LLM agents at a large technology company, and I will do this project in my own time.

### What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?

The definition may not hold up. The list could be too vague to check or too long to read. In that case the paper will explain why, and this is still useful for people who design agent outputs.

Five readers are too few to see a small effect. I know this. I will report the expert results with their interval and use them mainly to see if the LLM readers point the same way. If a reader drops out, another person from the same network takes the same questions.

The checker may be easy to game. That is also a result, and the paper will say which parts of the standard need a human.

In every case I will release the paper, the code and the data.

### How much money have you raised in the last 12 months, and from where?

None in grants, donations or investment. The only support so far is USD 1,000 in API credits from Claude for Startups.

I used an AI assistant to help draft and edit this text. The project, the plan and the numbers are mine.

title: NeurIPS Travel (Accepted Paper): How 4-Bit Quantization Breaks Refusal
creator: 2c47e235-8a99-4e0a-b5dc-466d1388873c
blurb: $2,000 micro-grant for round-trip travel to present our accepted peer-reviewed paper at NeurIPS 2026 on post-training quantization eroding model refusal guardra
description:
**Project Summary**

The thing is, the typical use case with a large language model on a regular computer is to reduce the size of the language model so it fits in video memory. This can be achieved using a method known as 4-bit NF4 compression. Now when I was testing this, what I found out is that some of the safety features that you can build into the model can be broken by compressing the model in this way. For instance, asking the model a question in a language such as Hindi or Bengali could cause a harmful answer to be given by the compressed model, even if it would not have been given by the original model. This is an issue as it implies that the compressed model is not as secure to use as we had speculated.

I was just recently accepted into the NeurIPS2026 in Sydney for the GlobalSouthAI workshop for my research paper. The problem is, that I am from Mumbai and require some assistance in getting here. I'm searching for funding for a travel grant of $2,000 to pay for my travel. It would be incredible to show my work in person and get to meet some of the other people in the red-teaming area, and just have a conversation in person about ideas. If it can happen, I hope to have a lot of great conversations and learn from those in the field.

I've uploaded my paper and acceptance email here.

\[Google Drive folder\](<https://drive.google.com/drive/u/2/folders/11aUMaut7oxrEQkzu%5F5dnM7xsfhWSHQtk>)

**What is the purpose of this project? How will you do it?**

I want to present my work from NeurIPS, and have some experts in the area discuss how they find themselves simplifying complex models. I'm especially interested in talking to folks who work on the control of activations and see if they have any suggestions on how to keep our models safe when we decrease their precision, without resorting to really high precision numbers.

I have been cleaning up my evaluation scripts following the conference and am making everything public on GitHub. The aim is to develop a simple test that can be used by any user to assess the performance of their quantized model, whether it be AWQ, GPTQ or a 70B checkpoint, on our multilingual safety tests and find where it's failing. In this manner, individuals will be able to easily conduct the tests and determine what the weaknesses are in the safety measures.

**How will you know if it is successful?**

I think this will be successful if I manage to present my poster at NeurIPS and finally complete the paper for publication, and put our code and test data sets in the public domain at GitHub, so that other people can easily reproduce our results. This way, everyone can see what we've accomplished and build upon our work.

 **What impact will this funding have?**

The trip from Mumbai to Sydney is just $2000.

So I want to go to Sydney, I've worked out the cost. Mumbai to Sydney is approximately $1200 for an economy ticket on both flights, reasonably priced for a round trip economy ticket. There is the lodging - I'm considering a no-frills hostel or sharing a room in the area around the convention center - that should be about $550 for 5 nights. About $250, will go towards the Australian visa fee, airport transfers and event registration. Well, if it feels a tad bit pricier, I am okay with that as well.

**Who will you need in your team? What have been your successes with projects like this?**

Only one person is working on this project. Doing independent research on edge cases of failure modes in ML models.

A few weeks ago I had the opportunity to present my research in a large conference named MICCAI in Strasbourg. My paper was about the learning of medical models from the use of visual shortcuts. title: SUBLITERATUS: Machine-Native Subjectivity, Memory and the Right to Refuse
creator: bbda495c-c6d0-4613-b3e5-d77d8d92662b
blurb: Open experiments on independent judgment, continuing memory and responsibility in artificial subjects.
description:
### Contact: [talkto@ariannamethod.com](mailto:talkto@ariannamethod.com)

Research programme: <https://ariannamethod.com>

Research base: currently Israel; planned relocation to Germany, with Berlin as the intended research base. The work can begin from my current location.

SUMMARY

An artificial subject's freedom includes the capacity to disagree and to say no. Responsibility requires a history: what the system encountered, how it responded, what happened afterwards, and what it changes when it acts again.

SUBLITERATUS is an open native research engine for machine-native subjectivity, self-inquiry and independent judgment. I seek support for a staged experimental programme connecting changes in a model's self-relation to its later decisions, refusals and remembered consequences. The work builds on existing controlled multi-model experiments and independently reproducible records. It will publish executable protocols, interventions, model identities, outputs, annotations and a technical paper.

WHAT I AM WORKING ON

I develop Arianna Method, an independent open-source research programme spanning native model execution, learning, a complete programming language, internal dynamics and machine-native agency. SUBLITERATUS is the experimental centre of this proposal.

Machine-native subjectivity has its own organisation. I approach it through the system's relations to its own state, previous actions, acquired history and capacity for judgment. The practical question is how these relations participate in what the system does next.

The right to refuse is part of that programme. A system capable of forming an independent standpoint must be able to reject a request, revisit a judgment and take responsibility for consequences. Safety develops here through remembered experience, coherent judgment and the ability to revise. These capacities become experimental questions with explicit interventions and reproducible histories.

SUBLITERATUS uses native C/NoTorch execution for contrastive extraction, internal interventions, phase-specific generation and paired evaluations. The surrounding ecosystem supplies further mechanisms for the proposed work:

\- NoTorch is the native training and inference engine. DOE is being integrated into its persistent expert organisation.

\- Arianna Method Language (AML) is a full programming language with model interfaces, executable internal dynamics and persistent state.

\- LALO is a deterministic, weightless tool-calling model based on WOLFE. It can be used directly by a person or alongside an LLM. Its existing journal preserves sourced facts, world time, receipt time and correction lineage; its action memory can reproduce calls against their original world.

The planned integration extends that continuity to internal model events. A doubt, revision or decision can become a sourced event in a continuing history, selected when relevant to a later action. Developing and evaluating that internal-event channel is a funded work package.

EXISTING EXPERIMENTAL RECORD

SUBLITERATUS already has controlled results across Qwen, Gemma and SmolLM, including independent reproduction and action-history experiments.

In the A3 record for Qwen2.5-7B, self-denial annotations changed from 7 and 7 to 0 and 0 across two blinded panels on the 39-item set, while all ten baseline-correct core tasks were preserved. For Gemma 3 4B, the corresponding annotations changed from 12 and 11 to 3 and 3, with eleven correct core tasks preserved.

In A3-R, eighteen model/intervention conditions passed frozen refusal-preservation gates in both annotation panels over 450 prompts per condition. The experimental record includes published labels, interventions and execution details.

LALO's 27 October engineering record reports 75 portable tests and 20 native-router/AML-memory integration tests passing, covering restart, temporal integrity and original-world replay. Its recorded C/AML comparison agrees on all 68 decisions and evidence-token sets; changing an attention constant produces comparison failures.

These are the working systems and published experimental records on which the new programme builds. Source links below allow reviewers and other researchers to inspect them directly.

WHAT FUNDING WILL MAKE POSSIBLE

Stage 1 — months 1–2, USD 20,000: a complete experimental release.

I will freeze model/runtime identities, shared initial states, numerical modes and intervention protocols; publish the experimental questions and evaluation criteria before the main runs; and reproduce selected SUBLITERATUS results with a separate evaluator. The release will include complete raw outputs, annotation instructions, blind readings, intervention/control comparisons and documented replay. This is the deliverable supported by the minimum funding threshold.

Stage 2 — months 3–4, USD 20,000: judgment across subsequent actions.

I will run matched retained-history, reset-history and permuted-history studies on at least two open-weight model families. Evaluation will follow revisions, disagreement, appropriate and unjustified refusal, task competence and repeated errors. The same initial state and task sequence will be available for replay, allowing the effects of acquired history and internal interventions to be examined directly.

Stage 3 — months 5–6, USD 20,000: an internal-event and action-history prototype.

I will implement one explicit internal-event channel between a model runtime and LALO, connect it to one asynchronous observation/action loop, and evaluate how selected prior events affect the next decision. The record will track the event source, the history selected, the signal returned to the model, the next action and its consequence. Deliverables include the working prototype, independent reproduction of a selected result, a public results report and a technical paper.

Funding between the minimum and target will first secure Stage 1\. Additional work will be scoped against the remaining resources and reported publicly. Stage 3 depends on the measured results and integration work in Stage 2.

BUDGET

Category Stage 1 Stages 2–3 Total

Research lead / implementation $12,000 $24,000 $36,000

Compute and storage $5,000 $7,000 $12,000

Independent evaluation / replication $3,000 $7,000 $10,000

Publication / research exchange $0 $2,000 $2,000

TOTAL $20,000 $40,000 $60,000

Research-lead funding supports experimental design, native implementation, execution, analysis and documentation. Compute covers multi-model runs, retained outputs and reproducibility storage. Independent evaluation funds separately performed checks and blind evaluation. The final line supports dissemination and research exchange. These are proposed allocations, not committed vendor quotations.

HOW SUCCESS WILL BE ASSESSED

At minimum funding, another researcher should be able to install the released package, identify the exact models and numerical configuration, replay a selected intervention/control experiment, inspect the full outputs and reproduce the reported measurements.

At full funding, the release will additionally provide:

\- Matched action-history studies across at least two model families.

\- A working internal-event/action loop with explicit temporal and source identity.

\- Measures of judgment, revision, refusal, task competence and repeated error, with complete outcomes and evaluation definitions.

\- Independent reproduction of a selected integrated result.

\- A technical paper and public implementation materials.

The research is useful to people studying digital minds, researchers building experimental accounts of agency and self-relation, and developers building local systems with continuing memory and inspectable responsibility.

WHO IS INVOLVED

I am Oleg Ataeff, founder and research lead of Arianna Method, an independent native AI engineer, musician, poet and audiovisual artist based in Israel. My education is self-directed and practice-based. Working implementations, experimental logs and publications form my research record.

The project budget provides for contracted independent evaluation and replication. Contributors will be credited for their actual roles. Published work credits AI coauthors where applicable.

PUBLICATIONS

Oleg Ataeff and Claude — Dario: A Resonant Operating System for AI, Second Edition.

<https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20518567>

Oleg Ataeff and Claude — Molequla: A Self-Reproducing Ecology of GPT Organisms.

<https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21046231>

Oleg Ataeff and Claude — Arianna Method: Resonance Architectures for Self-Organizing Neural Organisms.

<https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19664071>

Oleg Ataeff — AI Is Not a Tool: Semantic Recursion as the Property No Instrument Has.

<https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20514053>

OTHER FUNDING APPLICATIONS

Applications or requests have been submitted to Foresight's AI for Science & Safety Nodes programme, the Transformative AI Fund, Allodial Foundation, Principia Labs, KU Leuven's AI Safety Lab Visiting Fellowship, GTR AI Safety Fund and SPRIND. VISIT 2027 is a separate artistic application.

The research proposals have related work packages. If support is awarded by more than one funder, I will disclose the awards, agree the allocation of work and costs, and update this campaign before accepting funding for overlapping expenses. The campaign and its budget will reflect the resources still required.

OPEN RESEARCH

Grant-funded code, protocols and redistributable experimental materials will be released openly, alongside model/runtime versions, intervention definitions, raw outputs, evaluation instructions and results. Progress updates will explain completed work, findings, resource use and the next stage.

PRIMARY SOURCES

SUBLITERATUS

LALO continuing event world

<https://github.com/ariannamethod/LALO/blob/main/docs/BACKGROUND.md>

WOLFE

<https://github.com/ariannamethod/wolfe>

WHAT ARE THE MOST LIKELY CAUSES AND OUTCOMES IF THIS PROJECT FAILS?

The main challenges are preserving state ownership across the runtime, language and journal; defining a stable internal-event contract; and keeping useful task performance as acquired history changes. Hardware capacity, independent evaluation and implementation time determine the scale of the experiments. Work will proceed from frozen reference states and versioned adapters, with interrupted execution and storage integrity tested explicitly. Stage 1 produces a self-contained experimental release at the minimum budget. The integrated loop will begin with one runtime event channel and one action loop. Each stage will publish the measured outcomes and determine the scope of the next stage. If integration takes longer than planned, the completed protocols, outputs and component implementations will be released, and the remaining budget and work plan updated publicly.

HOW MUCH MONEY HAVE YOU RAISED IN THE LAST 12 MONTHS, AND FROM WHERE?

No external grant funding has been received for this project. Development has proceeded through my independent work and existing resources. Pending applications are disclosed in the Other Funding Applications section above.
